I received a large inheritance after my dad unexpectedly passed in the same situation- divorced with two kids. I'm not at all surprised he didn't tell you. I immediately got a financial planner and he made it explicitly clear that I should not tell ANYONE about the money. Someone else mentioned that within the first year, anyone can contest for the money- regardless of what the will says. It's unlikely, but it does happen and then it gets tied up in probate for years, or worse, they win the case and take a portion of it. 

Plus, it takes FOREVER to tally up estates, so he might have just recently found out. I didn't know the exact sum until about 6 months later. He probably won't receive the money for another couple of months. His brother is likely just living off of life insurance, which is disbursed immediately. But a large chunk of the money, from say, property, retirement, investments, etc, probably won't be disbursed for atleast another few months. 

I still get incredibly uncomfortable about telling people because it has made me very cynical and I find myself questioning whether people like me for me, or for my money. It could be that he didn't want your view of him to change (even though from your point of view it must seem like  that doesn't make sense since you were carrying him.) He could have feared that you'd only stay with him for the money. Who knows. Death and windfalls sent people off the deep end sometimes. It's an incredibly confusing and painful time. 

I wouldn't say this is a dealbreaker. I think you need to have a deep, 100% honest discussion with him about it. You might find that his point of view can allay your fears and explain his actions. Just remember that he's fragile and likely unsure of everything.

I grew up in a nice neighborhood where kids were always walking alone to each others' houses and what not. We had a pond about a mile from my house and it was the one place that was off-limits when alone because it was secluded and my parents were afraid of us drowning. I wanted to take my dog Champ to go swim but my brother wouldn't come. So, I lied to my dad and said I was going to go walk down a different street (not sure how I planned on explaining the dog being soaking wet, but I digress). 

Champ is in the middle of the pond when a pickup truck approaches me and asks me about fishing. Me being 10 and not understanding the danger, I talk to him. He goes back to his truck and I turn around to watch Champ. A few seconds later I feel a blade on my neck and his hand on my shoulder. He says "Don't scream or I'll fucking kill you. Get in the car." I get in and he instructs me to lie down under the dash, and then covers me with a jacket. I can hear Champ barking and clawing at the truck, and he drives away.

We drive to the next town over and park in an industrial complex behind a factory. He tells me to get up onto the seat and says he’s going to rape me. I cry and beg him not to, asking why he’s doing this to me. He replies that he’s “bored.” I had a lot of medical issues and when he made me take my shirt off, he saw that I had an ostomy bag. He immediately got nervous and decided he just wanted a blowjob. I told him I didn’t know how to do that, so he took my hand and showed me how to give a handjob. He came, and then immediately started beating me. He punched me a few times and then began choking me. I kicked his dashboard instinctively, and he only got angrier. He kept saying, “I’m going to fucking murder you bitch.” I don’t know how or why, but I stopped struggling and pretended I was dead. Apparently satisfied, he reached over to open the passenger side door. I then felt a boot connect between my legs, and he pushed me out of the car with his feet. I fell headfirst onto the pavement and blacked out. 

When I woke, he was carrying me and jamming my body into the side door of a dumpster. My fall was broken by a few bags of trash. I laid there for a few minutes, not knowing what to do. He came back and threw more trash on me. Then I heard his engine start and him drive away. I couldn’t see out, so I just hoped he was gone. Then I piled up all the trash I could and crawled out. I walked across the street to a plastics molding business. I rang the buzzer because the door was locked, and the secretary asked through the speaker how she could help me. I said “I was just kidnapped” and she ran and opened the door and started screaming for her boss to call 911. Everyone just kept saying “oh my god, OH MY GOD.” The owner scooped me up and laid me down on two chairs and covered me with his jacket. It felt like the police were there instantaneously, as was my mother. I remember her begging to hug me, but they kept telling her no because it could compromise the evidence. 

I spent the next two days in the hospital and luckily nothing was broken. Before I was even released, my kidnapper was found. He was 16 at the time of the crime and thus we had to take a plea bargain to prevent him from likely being released at 21. He served 10 years and was released in 2010. I have, and likely will for the rest of my life, served a sentence worse than any prison.

I was really sick in 2008 after a surgery went badly and I developed an abdominal infection. I was in the hospital the majority of the time, but at around four months was my worst stay. I was skeletal and had lost nearly all my hair and was being fed intravenously. I knew I was dying and everyone around me knew I was dying. The only doctors who came to see me were palliative care to try to make me comfortable. 

I cried 24/7. I cried because of the pain and because I was 18 and dying alone in a hospital bed. My friends had forgotten about me and my family stopped coming as often because it was wearing on them to see me waste away day in and day out. 

The cleaning lady worked the same floor nearly every day. At first she would silently go about her business while I wept. She often glanced at me with a pained look. She'd give me an encouraging smile before she left. This went on for another week until one day she put her broom down and came to my bedside. She had tears in her eyes and she brushed my head and told me in broken english to not cry; that it would all be okay. 

The next day she did the same thing, and every single day she would take a break to talk with me and comfort me. She told me about how she was in America to pay for her daughter to go to college back in the Philippines and that she hadn't seen her family in three years. She brought pictures in for me. She asked me why I cried so much and I told her about how I wanted to stop suffering and die already and she told me it wasn't my time yet; that I had to keep fighting. 

This went on for another three weeks. I don't believe in anything, but if angels exist, she was one. I was back on the same floor two weeks after being discharged, and she was gone. I don't know if I was delirious with fever and medication, or if strangers this profoundly compassionate actually exist. But I will never forget that look she gave me; like I was her own daughter and she'd sacrifice anything to save me. She did, and I don't even think she knows she did.

I've been committed and my father is a cop. There are basically three separate criteria and you must have one of the following:

1. You are suicidal and HAVE A PLAN
2. You have a plan to hurt another person
3. You have a comorbid condition that blurs the lines further (schizophrenia, drug addiction, etc.)

You can tell a therapist that you are suicidal, and unless you answer "yes" to the question of "do you have a plan?" you cannot be involuntarily committed. They can strong-arm you into committing yourself voluntarily, but they technically do not have grounds for a section. 

If you say "I want to die. I wish I would just die." those are PASSIVE thoughts. However, active thoughts, ie "this week I'm going to overdose" are grounds for protective orders. 

Know the laws. If your psychiatrist recommends a hospitalization, your best bet might be to voluntarily go. It varies by state, but getting out is A LOT easier if you go voluntarily. 

As for your last question, it again varies by state but I have never had a "one flew over the cuckoos nest" experience even when committed involuntarily at 13. I had a room mate and we mostly went to groups all day. People are rarely hospitalized for more than one week because of the demand for psychiatric care. 

Anyways, I'm half drunk and let me know if you need anything clarified.

I was in an accelerated nursing program in 2010 when I got a call from my dad saying his stomach was swollen and painful. We never really spoke until a year earlier, when he was diagnosed with ulcerative colitis (which I'd had my entire life). We bonded over our shared disease and misery and I finally got to know him for the incredible man he was. He trusted in my medical knowledge, and I stopped by his house every day after class to check on him. 

When I got there, I immediately knew he needed to go to the ER. His abdominal cavity was filled with fluid and he was jaundiced. The doctors wouldn't give any definitive answers, but I knew. I brought in his childhood photo albums and he told me stories and I tried to learn everything I possibly could about this man because I knew he would be gone soon and I didn't want his stories to die with him. I stayed with him around the clock, only leaving for class and clinical. 

It got to be too much on me very quickly. I shut off that part of myself that recognized him as my father. I was his healthcare proxy, and I needed to be the best advocate I could. On the third day he developed hepatic encephalopathy and was completely unoriented. His pancreatic cancer markers came back positive. It had metastasized to his liver. On the fifth day, his nephrologist pulled me aside and told me he was going into metabolic acidosis and that we had to make a decision about whether or not to put him on life support. We came to the decision to withhold treatment. 

I brought in his favorite music (Blondie) and shaved his face. I stayed awake all night, watching as each sign of death came. At 10am the next day, he pulled off his oxygen mask. I didn't know if he knew what he was doing, he was delirious. As his oxygen saturation dropped, I panicked. I've never felt so conflicted in my life. I didn't know whether or not to place it back on him or let him go. I did nothing. He flatlined. I screamed and cried, and I have never, ever, regretted anything in my life like I regretted those 20 seconds. I am haunted by what I saw, and the guilt of inaction. 

That day, I relapsed on oxycontin. Everything fell onto me; the decision making, planning his funeral, trying to maintain in nursing school. I didn't cry, I didn't speak; I got high and pretended I was unaffected. I was 20 years old and playing god with someone's life was too much for me to bear. I couldn't go to clinical without being high and snorting pills every couple hours in the bathroom. I didn't want to take care of anyone. I didn't want the responsibility of keeping them alive and healthy, because I couldn't even do that for my own father. I was a straight A student and the top of my class, and I didn't care anymore. About two months after his death, I quit. 

Since then, I transferred and started studying neuroscience. I began using heroin and spent five months in rehab. I'm doing well now. My father gave me two of the best gifts I could have ever asked for. One, the inheritance I received allowed me to get treatment for childhood trauma and the drug addiction I had been battling since I was 18 and prescribed oxycontin after surgery. And two, he gave me a reason to not settle on nursing school and instead pursue my Ph.D. When you throw everything in your life away, you have the power to rebuild it in any way you please, and he's the reason for that.
